title: Interior, exterior, and boundary
section: Point-Set Topology ▷ The Interior, Exterior, Boundary, Limit Points, and Closure of a Set

exposition.text:
The interior int A is the largest open subset of A; the exterior is int(X \ A). A point lies in
the boundary ∂A when every neighborhood meets both A and its complement. Thus ∂A =
A ∩ X \ A = A \ int A.
Interior, boundary, and exterior partition X. The boundary is closed and is unchanged on
replacing A by its complement. A set is clopen when it is both open and closed; equivalently,
it has empty boundary. Dense sets can have empty interior and a very large boundary: both Q
and its complement have boundary R.
Boundaries obey ∂(A ∪ B) ⊆ ∂A ∪ ∂B, with possible strict inclusion. If A is open or closed, its
boundary has empty interior, and therefore ∂(∂A) = ∂A. This last identity need not hold for an
arbitrary set, such as the rationals.

solution.text:
The closure is [0, 1] ∪ [2, 3] and the interior is (2, 3). Subtracting the interior gives [0,1] ∪
{2, 3}, since rational and irrational points are both dense in [0, 1].

The exterior is the complement of the closure. The only extra limit point of the reciprocal
sequence is 0, and [2, 4) adds the limit point 4. This description also includes the many
open gaps between consecutive reciprocals.

question.text:
For arbitrary subsets A, B of a topological space, which inclusion always holds?
(A) ∂(A ∪ B) ⊆ ∂A ∪ ∂B (B) ∂A ∪ ∂B ⊆ ∂(A ∪ B)
(C) ∂(A ∪ B) ⊆ ∂A ∩ ∂B (D) ∂A ⊆ A
(E) ∂A ∩ ∂B = ∅

solution.text:
If a point lies outside both boundaries, it has neighborhoods on which membership in A
and in B is separately constant. Their intersection makes membership in A ∪ B constant,
so the point is not on its boundary. Equality can fail: A = Q and B = R \ Q each have
boundary R, while their union has empty boundary.

question.text:
What is the boundary of Z in R?
(A) R \ Z (B) R (C) ∅ (D) {0} (E) Z

solution.text:
The integers form a closed set with empty interior. Hence their boundary, closure minus
interior, is the whole set Z.

question.text:
If A is a closed subset of R, which statement must be true?
(A) ∂A = ∅ (B) ∂A is open. (C) ∂(∂A) = ∂A (D) ∂A = int A (E) ∂A = A

solution.text:
Since A is closed, ∂A = A \ int A is closed. It has empty interior: a nonempty open set
contained in it would be an open subset of A, hence contained in int A, a contradiction. Its
own boundary is therefore itself. Closedness matters; for A = Q, the first boundary is R
and the second is empty.
